[[Image:Centaurea nigra Sturm24.jpg|thumb|Illustration]]'''''Centaurea nigra''''' is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Asteraceae]], and is also known as '''lesser knapweed''', '''common knapweed''', '''black knapweed''' and '''bell weed'''.

It is native to central [[Europe]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Centaurea nigra L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:191100-1 |access-date=2025-02-09 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> and has been introduced to temperate [[North America]] and [[Australasia]], where it is usually regarded as a [[noxious weed]] due to its fast spread, hardiness and competitive potential. 

==Description==
''Centaurea nigra'' is an upright [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] growing up to c. 1 m (3.3 ft) in height.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Black Knapweed, Common Knapweed, Knapweed, Lesser Knapweed, Spanish Buttons, Horse-knops |url=https://weeds.org.au/profiles/black-knapweed-common/ |access-date=2025-02-09 |website=weeds.org.au |language=en-AU}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Common knapweed {{!}} The Wildlife Trusts |url=https://www.wildlifetrusts.org/wildlife-explorer/wildflowers/common-knapweed |access-date=2025-02-09 |website=www.wildlifetrusts.org |language=en}}</ref> It produces spreading [[Rhizome|rhizomes]].<ref name=":0" />

''C. nigra'' initially produces a basal [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]] of leaves, which are usually [[Glossary of leaf morphology|entire]] and up to 30 cm long (11.8 in).<ref name=":0" /> Once the rosette is fully formed, it produces upright stems before eventually dying away.<ref name=":0" /> These upright stems turn purple when mature. The leaves on these stems are smaller, 1–8 mm x 2–10 mm, usually entire, grey-green and roughly hairy.<ref name=":0" />

The [[inflorescence]] is globe-shaped, 10–20 mm x 30–40 mm, and contains small purple to reddish flowers that are fringed by black or dark brown [[Bract|bracts]].<ref name=":0" />

The fruit (seeds) are a light brown flattened ovoid 3–4 mm long, topped with short bristles c. 1 mm.<ref name=":0" /> In its native range, flowering occurs in summer to autumn from June-July until September.<ref name="The Wild Flower Key">{{cite book|last=Rose |first=Francis|author-link=Francis Rose|title=The Wild Flower Key|year=1981|publisher=Frederick Warne & Co|isbn=0-7232-2419-6|pages=386–387}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Harris |first=M. |year=2017 |title=A morphological analysis of Centaurea nigra and its associated taxa in Hertfordshire |journal=New Journal of Botany |volume=7 |issue=2 |page=170}}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:Centaurea nigra 019.jpg|thumb|left|[[Deschambault-Grondines]], [[Quebec]], Canada]]
''Centaurea nigra'' boasts high nectar and pollen production relative to other British perennial meadow flowers.<ref name="Meadows">{{cite journal |last1=Hicks |first1=DM |last2=Ouvrard |first2=P |last3=Baldock |first3=KCR |date=2016 |title=Food for Pollinators: Quantifying the Nectar and Pollen Resources of Urban Flower Meadows |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=11 |issue=6 |article-number=e0158117 |bibcode=2016PLoSO..1158117H |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0158117 |pmc=4920406 |pmid=27341588 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Nectar, pollen and seeds are highly important food resources to many species of invertebrates and birds. In its native range, ''C. nigra'' can therefore greatly improve biodiversity values and ecosystem services, such as pollination, when planted with a variety of other [[Forb|forbs]], for example on field margins.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Critchleya |first=C. Nigel R. |last2=Fowberta |first2=John A. |last3=Sherwoodb |first3=Ann J. |last4=F. Pywell |first4=Richard |year=2006 |title=Vegetation development of sown grass margins in arable fields under a countrywide agri-environment scheme |journal=Biological Conservation |volume=132 |pages=1-11 |via=Elsevier Science Direct}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vickery |first=Juliet A. |last2=Feber |first2=Ruth E. |last3=Fuller |first3=Robert J. |title=Arable field margins managed for biodiversity conservation: A review of food resource provision for farmland birds |journal=Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment |volume=133 |issue=1-2 |pages=1-13 |via=Elsevier Science Direct}}</ref>

In its introduced range, ''C. nigra'' is often considered a weed because it excludes native vegetation and can reduce agricultural potential. In the United States, it invades meadows where it excludes native vegetation, thereby impacting native biodiversity.<ref name=":0" /> In Australia and New Zealand, ''C. nigra'' is known to invade grasslands, wastelands (e.g. railway lines, roadsides, waste areas) and agricultural lands.<ref name=":0" />

==Similar species==
Black knapweed is similar to brown knapweed (''[[Centaurea jacea]]''), spotted knapweed (''[[Centaurea stoebe|C. stoebe]]'') and greater knapweed ([[Centaurea scabiosa|''C. scabiosa'']]).<ref name=":0" /> It is also relatively similar to creeping knapweed (''[[Rhaponticum repens]])'' and star thistle (''[[Centaurea calcitrapa]]'').<ref name=":0" /> ''[[Centaurea ×moncktonii|Centaurea × moncktonii]]'', is a fertile hybrid between black knapweed and brown knapweed.<ref>{{cite web |title=Centaurea x_moncktonii in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250068128 |website=www.efloras.org |access-date=24 October 2022}}</ref>
